Verify an exit code directly, never through a pipe. 'cmd | tail; echo $?' reports tail's status. That error concluded a Thermite gate 'exits 0' on a missing tomllib when it exits 3, reached a PR description, and needed a public correction. Note also that PIPESTATUS is bash-only and expands to empty under zsh, so it silently reports nothing.

A round-trip proves information preservation and is silent about coverage, because text a tool never touches is restored perfectly. The migration tool reported 382/382 files restoring byte for byte while failing to touch every one-line contract and 17 @bv-tagged clauses across 10 files. Pair reversibility with a completeness check that asks whether any input construct survived unchanged.

When a gate goes red, establish whose fault it is before fixing it. doc-drift failed on an RFC branch and looked pre-existing; running it on a worktree at the branch point showed it exits 0 there, so the drift was ours - editing registry.toml drifts the design doc that governs it. The fix is a manual re-pin of audited-content-sha256 with a dated note keeping the prior entry, which is the convention that file already uses.

Environment, in this repo. verus is not on PATH and every forge check needs it: fetch release/0.2026.05.24.ecee80a arm64-macos from verus-lang/verus, about a minute. macos_allow_gatekeeper.sh EXITS 1 when there is no quarantine attribute, which is normal for a curl'ed archive, so check 'verus --version' exits 0 rather than trusting the script. cadical is absent, so EprSolverUnavailable is a missing binary rather than a language failure. Python 3.9 lacks tomllib, so the registry gates report inconclusive and exit 3 rather than failing: use 'uv run --python 3.11'.

Branch discipline in this fork. main carries the process layer - .claims/, .claude/, tooling/thermite3-migrate - and none of it belongs in a pull request to Thermite, so cut upstream-bound branches from an upstream/* ref and never from this fork's main. anchor/implementation is cut from upstream/rfc/full-words; rfcs/thermite-3-set from upstream/rfc/thermite-3. One PR per RFC, one commit per RFC so the revision derives from git, and never squash-merge an RFC PR or the review history collapses.

The migration rewriter needs the UNPATCHED parser. It reads Thermite 2 source, so it needs a front end that still has req/ens/fx as keywords, and on anchor/implementation those are gone. tooling/thermite3-migrate therefore lives on main and path-depends on that branch's thermite-syntax; run it against a worktree of the work branch. Its bv feature is non-default and required, or every @bv-tagged clause is declined.

The nine witness atoms are published to .claims/ and their removal is scheduled, not permanent. I first judged them unpublishable because each carries an identical empty {"in":[],"out":[],"next":[],"done":[""]} and therefore no reasoning. That was the wrong test. 'Carries no information' and 'is load-bearing' are different questions: day doctor reports 18 atoms declared, of which nine ARE these witness subjects, and a fresh clone rebuilds .kan/ from .claims/ via kan restore - so an unpublished subject does not exist for the next developer at all. They are a functional input to day's vocabulary and its composition check, not documentation, and leaving them local would have made the process non-reproducible on clone while looking tidier. Also unfounded: kan slugifies the space in 'atom/spike spike-result' to atom_spike_spike-result, so there is no awkward-filename cost. They are TEMPORARY. The harness-agnostic cycle replaces claim-copying with a day pack install driven from the justfile, at which point day's vocabulary arrives with the pack rather than through .claims/, and these nine come back out. That removal is a step of THAT work, not a loose end - recorded here so the next session finds the reason rather than rediscovering the argument for deleting them.

Handoffs go in kan under agents/handoff/<thread>, not in a markdown file. agents/handoff/main is the main thread; a parallel agent line gets its own rkey. The md file this replaces (HANDOFF.md, now deleted) failed for a specific reason worth keeping: it restated the environment notes and the discipline traps that already live in practice, which day's session-start hook already injects. So it duplicated the injected context, and the copy could drift from the source with nothing to catch it. In kan the handoff carries only what is session-specific - current state, next work in order, and cautions that apply to the next filing decision - and everything durable stays a practice claim and is cited rather than restated. It is also append-only and signed, so successive handoffs accumulate as a readable thread instead of one file being overwritten, and a claim can be retracted rather than silently edited. Read it with agents/handoff/main (4 live claim(s)):

Editing a governed source file drifts EVERY design doc whose route digests it, not one. The fmt fix on chore/move-kernel-out touched forge/src/vacuity.rs and thermite-syntax/src/lib.rs and turned four docs red at once - .design/basis/09-option-result.md and 11-ergonomics.md, which digest the same set including both files, .design/forge/vacuity-triage.md on vacuity.rs alone, and .design/scaffold/workspace.md on thermite-syntax as a lib root. Two habits made that expensive to see. First, doc-drift prints one DRIFT block per doc followed by its indented pattern list, so piping the report through head silently hides later docs AND truncates pattern lists; the first read showed one drifted doc where there were four, and showed a pattern list short enough to make a doc look unrelated to the edit. Read the whole report, or grep for the DRIFT lines specifically. Second, the run at the branch point is what makes the attribution: 936e07e9 exits 0 with 59 CURRENT and no drift, b10edfa8 exits 1, so the omission was ours and not inherited. Same shape as the registry.toml case already recorded here - the gate is working, the fix is a manual re-pin with a note that keeps the prior value.

Two shell traps hit in one session, both of which produced a confident wrong answer rather than an error. zsh applies history modifiers to unbraced parameter expansions inside double quotes, so "$1:thermite-syntax/src/lib.rs" expands with :t taken as the TAIL modifier - git received 936e07e9hermite-syntax/... and errored, but the surrounding pipeline still printed IDENTICAL export sets (0 names), a vacuous pass from two empty sets. Quote the colon out - "$1":"path" - and make set comparisons print the COUNT alongside the verdict, so an empty-versus-empty match cannot read as agreement. The second is already recorded for PIPESTATUS and it recurred in the same shape: PIPESTATUS is bash-only and expands to empty in zsh, so cmd | tail; echo ${PIPESTATUS[0]} printed exit= with nothing after it. Both belong to one rule - a verification that can pass by producing nothing is not a verification.

A PR whose failure lives in its BASE cannot be cleared by re-running it. gh run rerun --failed re-uses the ORIGINAL merge commit rather than recomputing refs/pull/N/merge, so after merging the fix into main, PR 11 kept failing on exactly the drift that main no longer had. Only a push to the head branch creates a run against a freshly computed merge. Two consequences. First, when a PR is red on something it does not contain, check whether the finding is arriving through the merge commit - reproduce by merging the head into the CURRENT base locally, which is what actions/checkout builds. Second, a plan that says fix the base, then re-run, then push has the last two steps in the wrong order; the push is what re-tests, so anything queued behind green must be reordered to ride on it.

Do not reach for KAN_NO_KEYCHAIN=1 to get past the macOS keychain prompt in a workspace that already has an identity. kan refuses it, correctly: the repo has claims in its log and a root seed, and seed-rooting a workspace with no identity file but a non-empty log mints a SECOND identity. Two identities in one workspace means the one that signs is decided by environment and file layout rather than by intent, so authorship of everything written afterwards depends on which key wins the race. The keychain warning kan prints alongside a SUCCESSFUL write is advisory - plain kan kept working throughout. If the prompt ever actually blocks, the right moves are KAN_IDENTITY_FILE pointed at the existing key, or kan identity adopt --key <path>, not the no-keychain flag. A second signing role is a different and supported thing: kan identity role add <name> --key <path>, read back with --trust roles.

Signing roles are DEFERRED until kan 0.12, deliberately, not rejected. The case for them is real: this workspace has one author - did:key:zDnaekvyhd...ge2V, reported UNDECLARED by kan identity authors - so a human decision and an agent observation are signed by the same key and are indistinguishable in the log, which is a gap for a project whose thesis is that assertions should be attributable. What blocks adoption today is not the feature but its READ path: on 0.9.2-beta.1 a role-bearing log needs --trust roles, and every existing reader that omits it - day session-start fold, kan context, anything scripted - silently under-reports while looking complete. That is the same silent-omission shape this repo keeps getting burned by. 0.12 is expected to make the default trust posture everyone who has contributed locally, which removes the flag requirement and turns a migration into a plain feature. Until then: one identity, and roles are NOT to be used as a keychain workaround - that is what the WouldMintSecondIdentity guard exists to refuse.

PR 11, the in-tree kernel removal, is MERGED to staging main as 98049d7c. Decision and rationale, recorded because it was proactive rather than forced: doll is already removing kernel elements on the mainline Thermite repo, and this fork is already committed to a large reconciliation pass once Thermite 3 is fully staged, so holding the removal here only widens the gap that pass has to close. It merged 12 of 12 green. Immediate consequence handled rather than discovered: PR 14, the uv interpreter pin, was cut from 84d276e7 and re-pinned .design/build/bootable-multicore-kernel.md - a file this merge DELETES - so it hit a modify/delete conflict plus a competing re-pin of stage4-epr-reconstruction.md, two re-pins of the same line for different causes. Rebased onto the new main, dropped the deleted doc, resolved stage4 to main kernel-removal pin, and re-derived pins from the gate rather than by hand. That turned out to be right for a reason worth keeping: the two doc changes in the original uv commit were artifacts of the PRE-removal route set, and nothing in spec-routes.toml digests .github/workflows/ci.yml at all, so the uv commit legitimately needs no re-pin now. Verified after rebase that the change survived intact - .python-version present, 1 setup-uv step, 5 uv run in ci.yml, 11 in the Makefile, require_toml_reader present, and ZERO remaining run: python3 or run: tooling/reqs lines - because a rebase across a commit that edits the same file is exactly where a silent loss hides.

git grep -E does NOT honour \\b, and I hit it four times in one session, twice after recording it. Each time the failure mode is identical and dangerous: the pattern matches NOTHING and the zero reads as a clean result. It produced 0 of 78 design docs carrying v2 keywords when the answer was 63, 0 surface sites when the answer was 611, and 0 TokKind references one minute after reading TokKind::Req off the screen. Use -w for word boundaries, or drop the anchor and accept a superset. And pair every count with a CONTROL that must be non-zero - grep for requires, or for the literal TokKind::Req - because the whole class of error here is a search that reports clean by matching nothing. Two sibling traps from the same session share the shape: zsh applies the :t history modifier inside double quotes, so "$1:thermite-syntax/..." silently became a tail expansion and an export-set comparison passed on two EMPTY sets; and PIPESTATUS is bash-only, expanding to nothing in zsh. One rule covers all three: a verification that can pass by producing nothing is not a verification.

The exclusion rule for the surface migration, stated properly after getting it half right. A document is excluded when it describes a PAST STATE of the language, not when it merely predates the change. The first pass excluded thermite2-semantics.md - which self-describes as the normative home for the SHIPPED Stage-1 semantics - but migrated .design/thermite2-program.md, which is the same kind of document, so three lines describing v2 features moved into v3 vocabulary: dec lex and dec wf in the Stage 1 row, ens#k and dec wf in the Q6/Q7 open questions. RFC-6 does not retroactively change what Thermite 2 shipped. Restored on rfc/full-words as bcb914eb. The frozen v2 artifacts then moved to docs/v2/ as PR 15 - semantics.md, program.md and program.pipeline.json - because root and .design/ both implied they were live. Checked before moving rather than after: neither carries an audited-content-sha256 pin and neither appears in spec-routes.toml, so leaving .design/ costs no gate coverage. 57 inbound references across 18 files, rewritten most-specific path form FIRST so the bare thermite2-program.md spelling could not corrupt the .design/-prefixed one, and 15 docs re-pinned because the rewrite reached source comments as well as prose.

A type-directed rename is only as complete as the type system is authoritative over the name. RFC-17 renamed the clause vocabulary in the AST and asserted that cargo check exiting 0 IS the completeness proof, since an unrenamed site does not compile. That is true and it was not sufficient, and the two escapes cost two CI failures nothing local could see. First, a FROZEN DIGEST: forge/src/kernel_image.rs computes sha256(format!("{:#?}", function.contract)) and Rust derived Debug renders FIELD NAMES, so the rename moved the digest 3f525f14 to 756cd389 with no clause, span or effect changed. Second, a SERIALIZED FORM: forge audit --json keys its boundary rows from BoundaryContract field names via serde, so the rename re-keyed a manifest carrying manifest_version v1 - an external contract - and the test that caught it, audit_enumerates_primitives_in_the_tcb, PASSED locally and failed only in CI. Two further structs were affected, KernelCertificateBinding.fx and SpecFnDecl.dec. The rule: a name escapes the type system wherever something reads it that is not the compiler - a digest over a rendering, a serialized form, a diagnostic string, a golden file. RFC-6 hit the same shape from the other side with clause-names-as-data, which means this is not a property of either rename but of names that cross out of the type system. The fix for the wire formats keeps both properties instead of trading them: Rust fields carry the full word and #[serde(rename = "req")] holds the v1 spelling, since reverting the fields would have reintroduced the split the change exists to remove.

A handoff is MACHINE-LOCAL and must never be published. agents/handoff/<thread> lives in .kan/, which is gitignored, and it stays there: it is addressed to the next session in this checkout, not to anyone reading the project. Peer-to-peer coordination belongs in durable mechanisms built for it - issues, milestones, design documents, RFCs - not in a claim that churns 100+ lines a session against a tracked file. This CORRECTS the earlier practice note, which said handoffs go in kan under agents/handoff/<thread> and left publication implied; the handoff was published in this session and in the one before it. Unpublishing is two steps, because deleting the .claims/ file is not enough - kan publish --all resurrected it. Publication is state in the LOG, carried by Publication claims on the subject, so both had to be retracted before --all would leave it alone. The subject then reads [stale] rather than [published]. Note the cost accepted: .kan/ is gitignored, so an unpublished handoff exists only in this working copy and does not survive a fresh clone or a second machine. That is the right trade because a handoff that needs to survive a clone is really coordination, and coordination has better homes.
